I'm so glad that you're going to spend your morning with us. We are here for another episode of Alternatives Access, and I think it's going to be a really special episode. I have a friend and favorite colleague from H. I, g capital, Jordan Griffin, who's an executive managing partner and also the co-president of Tam, their Total Access Middle Market strategy. And I'm thrilled to get her to dive into the middle market and why it's going to matter for portfolios as we move into a more complex world. With that, we'll just get started. Jordan, thanks for joining us. I'm so excited to be here. I feel like I'm hanging out with you all the time. I love it. It's going to be a fun time. Jordan and I have actually had a conversation on the middle market a handful of times over the last couple of months, and I think what's been interesting is every single time we chat, I learned something new. Oh, good. And well, and I think that's because the middle market, there's so much there that I think gets taken for granted, almost. With that, I think we should just start with why the middle market is compelling and and really how you would define it. So if we jump to idea one, maybe we just spend a moment on this segment in this part of the market, the why why in particular that you've spent a number of years investing in this space? Let me first define it because everyone defines middle market differently for today's conversation. Think of total enterprise value of less than 1 billion. And you're absolutely right. Why now for middle market I think I'm stealing a line from you that you once said to me. It's really why always it really needs to be a core part of anyone's private equity portfolio. But let me simplify the middle market opportunity in three things one, it's scale, it's inefficiency, and it's white space for operational improvement. First and foremost, the middle market is a large and deep market and it's highly fragmented. There are over 535,000 companies globally that are total value of less than 1,000,200,000 just here in the US. Now that big of market sourcing is key and we can talk a bit about that today. But that is key. But in addition you just have a plethora of great businesses, market leaders, strong cash flowing businesses. But many, and I'm generalizing here a bit tend to be under managed. Now that presents two great opportunities. One, you can buy them cheaper, but to be paths and optionality for value creation is much wider with an under managed business. I also really like the cellar dynamics in the middle market. It's partnership focus versus valuation focus. So 70% of global GDP is driven by family owned businesses. And when they are thinking about selling certainly maximizing price is up there. But they're also thinking about their legacy. They're thinking about their culture fit. So that allows more of a relationship partnership aspect as a buyer. Sure. And then when you're dealing with a market this large and deep, of course it's going to be less efficient. It's going to be less transparent. I love that that leads to less competition. You're not going to see as many of these robust auction processes where everybody and their brother is bidding and they're bidding up, up, up into valuation, that's pretty untenable. That happens less frequently. 97% of off market opportunities are found within the middle market. So as you can see, there's a lot to love in terms of structural inefficiencies, but also opportunities that the middle market provides. Sure. I mean, a lot to love, but even more so just a lot to do. I think so many of our clients are now thinking about investing in private equity as a potential part of their portfolio for outsized returns or diversification, so on and so forth. But I think what's increasingly compelling here is this is what I would argue is maybe one of the truest forms of active management because of the ability to value, create, to partner alongside founders and families who may be looking to sell. So really interesting part of the market. What I want to make sure we sort of define in today's conversation is really that this is a subset of private equity. And so when our clients are maybe thinking about investing in the space more broadly in private markets, this is just one way to access private companies. There are plethora of other places that clients can continue to invest, but we'll spend some time diving in here. The next idea that I think is compelling, and you alluded to this, but it's really so many factors. But the reason why you invest in private equity is for the potential for outsized returns. Take us through what historical performance in this asset class has looked like. While we won't guarantee or promise what future returns will look like, I do think that history can be informative of sort of what you're looking at. And so maybe take us through how you're thinking about long term potential for outperformance, but also what historically the middle market has done. Yeah, absolutely. There has been tremendous outperformance in private equity as well as in the middle market. You know, I think all of us who are active investors in private equity, we really seek it out in our portfolio as a core allocation. But it's because it's able to deliver uncorrelated alpha relative to public equities. However, I don't know that everyone is focused on the middle market when they think private equity, and they absolutely should be. If you look at today's private equity market, 87% of deal volume based on deal count is in the middle market 87%. So if you're making an allocation to private equity and you're trying to drive for that alpha generation and you're only focus on large cap and mega cap, you're only seeing 13% of the market. And that comes into play not only on acquisition, but we'll talk a bit about exit. You know, in order to be successful and to drive that outperformance. To me it's sourcing. Well it's buying right. It's driving value creation and then having strong exit execution. But as you're looking at those four components, putting them all together is what's going to lead to this outperformance. If you see this chart here and we dissect the returns a bit going back to 2007, middle market private equity has delivered two and a half times greater growth than the S&P 500. But if we dissect that even further, it's not only outperforming public equities, but it's also outperforming mega cap growth equity buyout in general. And part of that is because it's such a large swath of the private equity universe. So I'm not saying you need to pick one or the other. I think it's really important that you do have a diversified portfolio within your private equity allocation. Well, and I think, too, in the spirit of diversification, I also think there is this layer of and I think sort of the natural next question is there's more opportunity here. You have the potential for outperformance, but is there also the potential for greater risk. So maybe just spend a quick moment on what the risk look like in this part of the market relative to maybe large cap, which most people are typically more familiar with? Right. Thinking about the idea that maybe a larger business is more insulated from some of the maybe the macro things that take place or management issues and so on and so forth. Yeah, absolutely. I think one way to look at risk in general is where are you buying a company? Sure. And so a lot of that comes down to your entry multiple. And within the middle market, we've been able to achieve a lot lower attachment points on the onset. So we're all familiar. In 2021 there is a huge value trap. People were overpaying and over leveraging for businesses. That is absolutely what you should try to avoid because it can occur during various market cycles. But if I go back to 2021 and I look at the entry multiples over the last five years, large cap was buying companies at 15.5 times entry multiple. The middle market is buying companies four times cheaper at 11.6 times. So what does that mean? That's actually a great springboard for downside protection but also asymmetric risk return on the downside protection area. If you are buying a company at eight, nine, ten times entry multiple, and you're getting your leverage for that company from private debt investors who are focused on downside protection themselves, they're not going to lend to you at high loan to value ratios. In fact, it's going to be moderate to low loan to value ratio. They're looking to protect themselves. And so we appreciate it's a smaller company. There's going to be lower leverage. So right there you're kind of avoiding the second part of that equation of over leveraging. But you're also less likely to overpay. And that four times cheaper valuation. It provides a bit of a valuation cushion. And it also helps absorb earnings shocks. But taking a step back it's not just about where you're buying it. You will tend to see middle market portfolios to be much more diversified in terms of the number of portfolio companies. So not anyone deal is going to make or break a fund, and not anyone deal is going to lose an entire fund. So I think that's a big mitigate. The opportunity set though is robust. You have significant pass in terms of the value creation playbook that you can apply to a company that you've bought at a ten times entry multiple, and that operational framework, which is going to lead to ultimately creating a very attractive value creation story. Increases also your paths on exits. And the best way to de-risk a portfolio is to exit a company. Well and I think to and you you talked us through idea three which is great. And so maybe we flash it for for everyone who wants to take in those data points. I think what's really nice about about this slide is, you know, you sort of make it really clear in entry at lower multiples, less leverage, just inherently really across the sector. But definitely that what you've been focused on is investor. You have all of the potential from a value creation perspective operational improvement but exits. And to really that takes us to our fourth idea. And we're just grooving this morning on this. But I think what's really interesting here is the last three years, every conversation I've had with clients who have invested in large cap private equity, for the most part, have had delayed or slow distributions relative to what they thought would be the case in the middle market. You haven't necessarily seen that, and I think that's because of less reliance on the IPO. Markets take us through the middle market specifically, and even the lower middle market in more particular just around exit opportunity, one with those exits can look like. But then also sort of the strategic levers you all have around exiting to, to different places. Yeah. As I mentioned, one of the best ways to de-risk your portfolio is to solidify your marks, to generate realizations, to distribute capital back to your investors. That's investor favorite part. And hopefully you're doing that at Target Returns or even better above target returns. But you want to be in control of your own destiny on the exit. You know, having just 1 or 2 paths can be very limiting. The beauty of the middle market is we have multiple paths to exit. Certainly, the IPO market is a path. It's not the biggest path. Definitely not a huge component. When you start talking about lower middle market companies. And as much as IPOs are really attractive, they're never exactly a full exit. Sometimes they're more of a capital markets transaction, but you could have the best company and have perfectly executed your value creation plan and you're ready to exit. And if that IPO window is shut and that's really your only path, then you're not able to de-risk your portfolio and you're not able to get distributions back to your clients. You're left hanging out a bit in the middle market, right? That is a path, certainly, but you're also very much selling to strategic buyers. You're selling to financial sponsors, larger private equity firms. And because of where the middle market sits, the number of upper middle market managers, large cap managers, even mega cap managers is enormous. So you have a much wider group of people to be potential buyers. And I think what's nice about what you're describing to we we had some recent conversations with some of our partners, and what they were describing is as it becomes harder or even less attractive to be a publicly traded company today, at least in the US, where it's a much more expensive endeavor than it was 20 years ago. Private equity markets have become incredibly efficient and also quite large. And so to your point, this ability to even sell up market to upper middle market or large cap sponsors is a really material exit opportunity because there are so many, but also because they're so large. The capital does exist in these markets today, which I think is pretty interesting. Absolutely. And if you look at just the statistics alone, the middle market has been incredibly active on exits. It does similar to how it makes up the large majority of deal volume at acquisition. It also makes up the large majority of deal activity.. Exactly 94% of exits that you have seen in private equity have occurred within the middle market based on deal count. That's a staggering number. Well, one of the things that you also alluded to, I guess, on our prior idea was the operational improvement or the value creation abilities. And I think that's what I want to spend the most time on today, because I think sometimes it's taken for granted that, you know, you don't just buy a company, cross your fingers and then look to exit at a greater multiple. And we all win, really. In particular, in the middle market space, there's work to be done. We're rolling up our sleeves. And so take us through idea five. And this is sort of this hands on operational approach. What does a value creation actually look like. Because it's not crossing your fingers and hoping. No it's definitely not. In fact, if you are relying on multiple expansion or financial engineering to be the hallmark of how you're going to drive returns, that will be a failed strategy in today's environment. And this has been a statistic that's been quoted pretty often recently. But in today's environment, if you're trying to hit a 20% IRR and a two and a half times cash on cash return, you have to grow annual EBITDA by 12% year over year. That is a huge shift from ten years ago. Where to achieve the same return, you only were required 5% growth. So what? That tells me, it tells me that the bar has risen, right? It tells me that you have to earn the return via hands on operational approach to value creation. That can take on a lot of different flavors. It can be accelerating revenues, operational efficiencies, or upgrading or building a management team. In the middle market, you see a fair amount of corporate carve outs. You are then lifting up an actual management team to that. But the more important aspect is identifying on day one. Why is it attractive to buy this company? What is it about this company that during our ownership we can effectuate change and drive value creation? And that value creation playbook shouldn't be aspirational. It needs to be highly achievable. Right? So when we're underwriting a business, we don't include multiple expansion and we don't include strategic M&A. Those are a bit outside of our control. We have a very systematic value creation. And each company requires a different approach. But it's identifying that and then also having the hands on expertise to execute it. It may be great that you've identified it, but if you don't have anyone that can deliver on it, that will also be challenging as well. And I think one of the things that has been interesting over time, as we've spent more time in the middle market in particular, is this idea around having a team large enough to your point to actually execute on something like this? Talk a little bit about it. Maybe we just lean for another moment into the risk here. In a world like today, when I think about inflation hovering where it is, interest rates kind of hanging out where they are and have been for the last year. How do these things impact the operational improvements you can bring to a company, even just in this world of AI? I would imagine that smaller companies have a harder time effectuate these things, and so a manager who can step in and bring value creation in this form could be really, really accretive to their already existing businesses because I mean, historically, right, you haven't invested in businesses that aren't already profitable, that are already revenue generating. Right. We're investing in good businesses from start. But what does that look like just being a smaller company. How they adopt change in this way? No, I think you're absolutely right. I mean, with smaller companies in and of itself, sometimes they're not kind of able to institutionalize it and take it to the next level. We love under managed businesses. We like to buy complexity, but we're ultimately trying to sell simplicity. And that's key. But having expertise where it's a repeatable playbook, where we've done it time and time again of identifying a company that has too much customer concentration. But we see a path, and we have operating partners to deliver on how we're going to diversify that customer concentration. That's a very achievable value creation lever that you can pull. I think AI is core to every underwrite that we do. It's core to every private equity managers underwrite that they do and is AI disruptor and something that is very difficult to solve and maybe outside of your control to solve. Or actually, is it a benefit and productivity tool? A smaller company is underutilized in that area, and bringing resources of very established private equity managers that can provide operating partners to institutionalize their AI approach is incredibly beneficial. Again, we talk about risk, and you do think of smaller companies as having greater risk, but in many ways, because you're buying it so much cheaper. You build in a buffer, and there's so much more to do with that business. If something's incredibly a well, well old machine and operating on all cylinders, you're sort of wondering where where am I going to get my 12% annual EBITDA growth? And that's the dynamic that I think is incredibly attractive in our market of it. Well, you've absolutely made the case for middle market. As always. I learned something new from you. I love this idea around entering complexity, selling simplicity. I'm going to steal that for me. But I think more importantly, just another lever for our clients to have in their toolkits or to pull on their own right. Knowing more about the private equity space and what you can do to diversify your portfolios. We're so focused on building in durability, particularly in markets that look like today. So hopefully you all take away some ideas as well. Jordan, I can't thank you enough for your time. It's been a pleasure for all of you who spent your morning with us, I appreciate it. Hopefully it was a great 20 minutes and we will catch you next time for all to access. Thank you for joining us. title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks - The Guardian
content: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger. Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters. Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”. JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported. He was commenting on the chancellor’s decision to raise the corporation tax surcharge on profits, known as the banking surcharge, to 6 per cent from 3 per cent, which could cost the bank an extra £120m in taxes. Speaking to a private banking conference, the veteran banker said that doubling the levy “lacks principle” and overlooks “a highly competitive global marketplace” for the banking industry. JP Morgan employs 23,000 people in the UK. The majority are in London, with 5,300 in Bournemouth and 4,000 in Glasgow and Edinburgh. Last November the Wall Street giant’s chief executive approved a new tower development in Canary Wharf, east London, but later warned that a tax raid raid on banks could force JP Morgan to “reconsider” the multibillion-pound plan if taxes in the UK became “too much”. Speaking to the JPMorgan European Financials Conference on Thursday, Dimon said his plan to offset the UK bank surcharge was “more in sorrow” than in anger. A JP Morgan spokesman last night declined to comment on Dimon’s latest remarks, which were first reported by the Financial Times. title: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattacks targeting third-party vendors - KERN Radio
content: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard disclosed Thursday that third-party service providers connected to their businesses were targeted in cyberattacks, potentially exposing limited customer information while leaving core banking and payment networks intact. The ransomware group known as n0n claimed responsibility for the intrusion and published stolen datasets online Thursday after an extortion deadline passed. None of the financial institutions identified the outside vendors targeted in the attack. The compromised records primarily consist of nonfinancial information, including customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and loyalty program engagement histories. According to a review of the leaked files, the Visa records centered on cardholders across Asia-Pacific markets such as Japan, Australia, Singapore and Hong Kong, whereas the Mastercard files involved benefit program enrollees in North America, the Middle East and Africa alongside a small number of employee email addresses. Separate leaks tied to JPMorgan Chase loyalty platforms reportedly affected roughly 16,000 individuals. All three companies emphasized that their internal infrastructure and payment processing systems were unaffected by the breach. A Mastercard spokesperson stated that the incident occurred “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses — non-payments information — from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” adding that card usage remained uninterrupted. Similarly, a Visa spokesperson noted that “there is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected,” while confirming the breach originated with an Asia-Pacific vendor. JPMorgan Chase also addressed speculation linking the data theft to recent online banking disruptions, clarifying that the two events were separate. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” a bank spokesperson said, noting that the earlier outage stemmed from a software bug and that the bank would offer complimentary credit monitoring to affected customers where appropriate. Visa echoed that its own vendor breach was “unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week”. Cybersecurity researchers tracking n0n say the fast-growing extortion gang has claimed roughly 200 victims since emerging in September 2026 and relies heavily on artificial intelligence tools to identify software vulnerabilities. Although sensitive payment card numbers and security codes were not exposed in this incident, security analysts warn that leaked names, contact details and bank affiliations give scammers credible material to launch targeted phishing campaigns.

title: Korea’s National Pension Service and JP Morgan AM sign business agreement - Funds Global Asia
content: The National Pension Service, South Korea’s state-run public pension fund and JP Morgan Asset Management have signed a MoU for a strategic alliance covering all asset classes at the JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York. This agreement was established to expand the existing entrusted management relationship into a relationship spanning all asset classes, including stocks, bonds, multi-asset and alternative investments. JPMorgan Chase is a global financial group that engages in financial businesses such as investment banking, retail banking, corporate finance and asset management. JPMorgan Asset Management has been managing the investment assets of the National Pension Service since 2015. Kim Sung-joo, chairman of the National Pension Service, and George Gatch, president of JP Morgan Asset Management, attended the signing ceremony on November 10. Earlier, Chairman Kim Sung-joo held a separate meeting with key executives and exchanged views on the outlook for global financial markets and ways to expand strategic cooperation between the two institutions. The two institutions plan to pursue the exchange of information and expertise regarding global macroeconomic and financial market trends, asset allocation, portfolio construction and risk management; research cooperation across all asset classes and strengthening of investment capabilities and exploration of additional cooperation measures aligned with the National Pension Service’s long-term operational goals. JPMorgan Asset Management plans to open a new local office in Jeonju in 2027 to expand its presence in Korea. title: Bank With Chase? New York Account Holders May Have Been Hacked - CNY News
content: You may want to change your account passwords if you bank with JP Morgan Chase. It's a good idea to change passwords regularly, regardless. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a cyberattack targeting third-party service providers exposed certain customer marketing data, though the financial giant explicitly denied rumors that the breach stemmed from a massive service outage earlier this week. According to statements released by the bank, attackers accessed marketing records held by unnamed external vendors. While the company stated its core banking systems were not compromised and services remain uninterrupted, the exposed vendor data may include customer names and email addresses. Chase emphasized that the incident has "no connection" to a separate software and transaction processing disruption that temporarily prevented thousands of customers from logging in or moving money earlier in the week. READ MORE: Patient Accounts Access After Quest Diagnostic Data Breach, What New Yorkers Should Know Meanwhile, cybersecurity researchers noted that a ransomware group known as "n0n" recently leaked a small dataset on the dark web allegedly tied to JPMorgan Chase. That leak reportedly contained roughly 16,000 customer email addresses—many linked to an invite-only credit card for ultra-wealthy clients alongside some phone numbers, account IDs, and over 100 employee emails. JPMorgan Chase has not confirmed the exact number of impacted individuals, noting it will directly notify affected customers and offer complimentary credit monitoring where appropriate. Security experts warn that the primary threat following an email exposure—especially right after a high-profile outage—is targeted phishing scams. Criminals frequently exploit moments when customers expect urgent updates from their bank. Watch for phishing: Never click links or download attachments in unexpected emails or texts claiming to be from Chase. The bank will never ask for your password, token code, or full Social Security number via email. Forward suspicious emails to phishing@chase.com. title: JPM Foresees XIAOMI-W 3Q Adj. NP to Dive 58%; Smartphone Demand Still Weak - TradingView
content: JPMorgan released a research report forecasting that XIAOMI-W 1810's adjusted net profit for 3Q will shrink 58% YoY. The broker forecast AI investment to drive operating expenses above expectations, partly offset by growth in smartphone revenue and stabilizing gross margin. It lowered its 3Q net profit forecast by 15%, estimating smartphone margins will trend toward stability, although demand is expected to remain weak. JPMorgan maintained a Neutral rating with a TP of HKD32. The broker said smartphone shipments have recorded both QoQ and YoY declines for four straight quarters. It forecasts full-year shipments this year to fall 24% YoY, with declines expected to continue in 1H27 before a mild recovery possibly emerges in 2H27 at the earliest. For AIoT, the broker predicted IoT revenue to decline 10% YoY in 2026, representing the largest drop among all segments, followed by another 3% decline in 2027. In the EV segment, October deliveries crossed 50,000 units, with SkyNomad accounting for more than half. JPMorgan forecast deliveries of 450,000 units in 2026 and 650,000 units in 2027, below market expectations of 700,000-800,000 units. Expansion into Europe in 2H27 could be a potential positive catalyst, although regulatory restrictions in 2028 may limit upside potential. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Visa (V), and Mastercard (MA) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor. Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident. JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. "We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added. A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region. "This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added. A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar. The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses. "The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement. The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November. title: Visa, Mastercard, and JP Morgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised - WBAL News Radio
content: Data from thousands of Visa, Mastercard and JP Morgan Chase customers was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, according to several reports. It’s the latest in a string of tech incidents that have unnerved customers across the U.S. over the past two weeks. Though the scope and source of the information remain unclear, The Wall Street Journal reports that thousands of customers’ data was involved. The incident has not disrupted payment services and is not linked to banking problems from earlier this week. JPMorgan Chase said Thursday that attackers targeted third-party service providers and may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses. The bank said the incident was not connected to service disruptions customers experienced earlier in the week. JPMorgan Chase did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party providers that were targeted. “Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” a JPMorgan Chase statement said. Visa also confirmed a security incident involving a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. Its own systems were not affected, and there was no indication that payment data, including card numbers, had been compromised, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. A Mastercard spokesperson said hackers accessed a limited amount of information belonging to some cardholders enrolled in a particular benefits program. The spokesperson said Mastercard contained the exposure and that its payment network and customers’ ability to use their cards were unaffected. The news comes after several days of technology outages across the U.S. disrupted air travel, email and hotel bookings, and compromised classified internal communications at the National Security Agency. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that an attack targeted a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. All three companies said their primary banking and payment systems were not impacted, but some customer information may have been accessed. J.P. Morgan said on ‌Thursday that third parties who provide services to the company were the target of ​a cyberattack. J.P. Morgan released a statement on X Thursday about the cyberattack. "We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses. There is no disruption to our services." Morgan experienced issues processing transactions earlier this week because of a problem which also impacted ​other banks ​and caused ⁠some disruptions. These incidents at J.P. Morgan come after several recent including a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground ​stop ⁠that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft's global email outage. title: Computacenter’s record order visibility supports growth outlook, says JP Morgan - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results JP Morgan has reiterated its constructive stance on Computacenter PLC (LSE:CCC), the IT services provider, after management discussions reinforced confidence in its growth prospects through 2027 and 2028. The bank retains an 'overweight' rating, with analyst Joseph George highlighting continued order-book expansion and record near-term visibility following a meeting with chief executive Mike Norris. The discussion took place at JP Morgan's UK Leaders Conference, where management outlined the opportunities from sustained investment in technology infrastructure. Long-term systems investment and incentives for the salesforce remain central to Computacenter's strategy for converting rising demand into further growth. Regional trading commentary was encouraging, with the UK delivering market share gains and Germany expected to perform better in the second half of 2026. France remains a turnaround priority, requiring further management attention as the group seeks to improve its performance in the market. JP Morgan views Computacenter's ability to serve infrastructure-intensive customers, including hyperscalers, as a competitive advantage over other value-added resellers (VARs). The bank also highlighted evidence of market share gains across several end markets, supporting its confidence in the company's underlying growth drivers. However, customer concentration and an increasingly project-led business mix remain important considerations for investors. JP Morgan expects next week's capital markets day to provide further insight into demand visibility and the strength of the order book. The event could offer additional evidence that the group's recent momentum can translate into sustained growth over the coming years. title: Is A Fed Hike Still Good News For JPMorgan? - Trefis
content: Most investors expect a Fed rate hike to be good news for big banks like JPMorgan Chase. Higher rates let a bank charge more on its loans. On our data, that still holds for the business. It does not hold for the stock. The short answer is no. Over 21 Fed hikes since June 2006, a fund of big financial stocks beat the S&P 500 in the next three months only 6 times. JPMorgan beat it after 8 of them. Since the latest hike, JPMorgan has lagged the S&P 500 so far, while that fund has beaten it. The Fed’s rise in the top of its target range to 4.0% took effect on Sept 17, 2026. It was its first increase since the one that took effect on July 27, 2023. From the close the day before through Wednesday’s close, JPMorgan returned -6.6%, counting dividends. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF, called SPY, returned -2.9%. Two other big banks did worse. Bank of America returned -15.5% and Citigroup -11.3%. Wells Fargo returned -6.5%, about the same as JPMorgan. Our data shows no single confirmed cause for these drops. JPMorgan has lost 6.6%, counting dividends, since the Fed hike that many owners expected to help it. If JPMorgan is a big part of your savings, that is a fall you have had to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record. They did, day to day. We measured how closely each stock’s daily move tracked the daily change in the 2-year Treasury yield. That yield follows where traders expect Fed rates to go. The measure is called correlation. A high positive score means the two moved together, and a score near zero means no link. From 2016 to 2019, the yearly score of the Financial Select Sector SPDR fund (XLF) averaged 0.52. JPMorgan’s averaged 0.51. In 2026 so far, XLF’s score is -0.09 and JPMorgan’s is -0.04. The SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (KRE), a fund of smaller banks, is at -0.19. Put simply, bank stocks no longer rise on days when rate expectations rise. SPY now has a negative score too, at -0.13. We think higher yields are trading as bad news for stocks in general. The table sets the old link next to this year’s, and next to each fund’s record after hikes. Source: Trefis analysis of Intrinio daily closes, FRED and Treasury.gov yields. Scores are correlations of daily returns with the daily change in the 2-year yield. Hike and any-day results compare total return over the next three months, from June 2006 on. Yes. Net interest income is what a bank earns on loans and bonds, minus what it pays on deposits. JPMorgan’s was $27.0 billion in the three months to September. That is 12.8% more than a year earlier. The quarter ended soon after the hike, so that growth came mostly before it. What it paid on deposits fell 2.0%. Peers grew too. Citigroup’s net interest income rose 13.7%. Bank of America’s rose 8.0%, and Wells Fargo’s rose 4.7%. The banks say rates still help. On its Oct 13 call, JPMorgan’s chief financial officer said the bank remains asset sensitive. That means its income tends to rise when rates rise. Bank of America said a rise of one percentage point above market expectations would add about $1.4 billion of net interest income over 12 months. Wells Fargo said it is modestly asset sensitive. So the business still earns more from higher rates, but the stocks no longer rise with them. On Oct 13, JPMorgan’s chief financial officer also said the market then priced one more hike in December. We think a hike that is widely expected is likely already in the share price. The link has broken before and returned. In 2022, XLF’s score was -0.13. It rose to 0.35 in 2023 and was 0.22 in 2025. JPMorgan also stands apart after sharp jumps in yields. Since 2006 we found 10 completed episodes when the 2-year yield rose a quarter point or more in a week. JPMorgan beat SPY over the next three months after 8 of them. Its median return was 11.7%, about 4.8 points ahead of SPY. The funds did not share that edge. XLF beat SPY after 5 of the 10 jumps and KRE after 4. XLF rose after 7 of them. That is close to its 66.0% rate of rising over any three months. So for the sector, a yield jump has not been a useful buy signal. The bank funds have also beaten the market over the past month. From Oct 19 to Nov 18, KRE rose 1.8% and XLF rose 2.5%, while SPY fell 4.7%. JPMorgan fell 2.8%. Our read: a Fed hike is not a reason on its own to buy bank stocks. JPMorgan closed at $324.11 on Wednesday. That is 11.1% below its 52-week high close of $364.68. Over the past year it returned 10.3%, close to SPY’s 11.8%. If rates do not drive the stock, other things do. Our Nov 3 piece looked at one of them. See Bank Stocks’ Real Risk Is A Credit-Card Rate Cap. For readers weighing a purchase now, see Should You Buy Bank Stocks After The Election? The same hike reads differently for tech stocks. For that side, see What Does A Fed Hike Mean For AI Stocks? The obvious story about rates has not been a reliable guide to bank stocks. We built our own strategy on records like these, and we would gladly hear from anyone who has found a better one. title: Wells Fargo reportedly hires JP Morgan card services chief Allison Beer as next COO - FinTech Futures
content: Wells Fargo previously revealed in September that current COO Scott Powell is moving to become CRO upon the retirement of Derek Flowers next year. Wells Fargo has reportedly poached Allison Beer from US rival JP Morgan Chase to serve as the bank's next chief operating officer (COO). This is according to a report by Bloomberg, which cites sources with knowledge of the appointment and states that Beer will succeed Scott Powell from early next year. Wells Fargo formerly announced in September that Powell will become chief risk officer (CRO) at the bank upon the retirement of Derek Flowers in January. Powell has held the COO position at Wells Fargo since 2019. Beer has worked at JP Morgan Chase since 2017. She has previously held the roles of head of digital and chief product officer, and currently runs the bank's card services and connected commerce business as CEO. In this position, Beer has helped direct a number of card programmes for JP Morgan Chase, including last year's Chase Sapphire Reserve credit card revamp and securing an issuing partnership for the Apple credit card. Related:Former NatWest CEO Dame Alison Rose joins Otoma board According to Bloomberg, Beer is now ending her tenure at the largest bank in the US to join Wells Fargo in 2027. Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf has worked to build out the bank's leadership team this year with the additions of Faraz Shafiq as head of AI products and solutions and Dennis Devine as head of business banking. title: Fixed income: A high-conviction opportunity - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Fixed income is both a diversifier and one of our highest-conviction ideas. Bond yields today are the most attractive they've been in twenty years, and that means something simple for investors: you can now earn a genuine total return from income alone, not just downside protection. Per J.P. Morgan’s 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA), global aggregate bond return forecasts have risen from a low of 2.1% in 2021 to 5.3% today, and global sovereign bonds offer their best return forecasts since the post-financial-crisis era. This is a structural shift, not a cyclical blip, and one investors can participate in today. The case is straightforward. Per the 2027 LTCMA’, the 10-year U.S. Treasury offers a 5.1% yield and a 10–15 year expected return of 5.5%; the 30-year offers a 5.4% yield and a 6.2% expected return. Investment grade (IG) credit yields 6.3% for a 6.1% expected return — the best in over twenty years — while high yield offers 8.5% for a 6.7% expected return, and emerging market debt offers 7.0% for a 6.5% expected return. These are the highest global bond return forecasts in two decades, and a decisive break from the unusually low returns of the post-financial-crisis era. The driver is structural: real yields have normalised, creating what the LTCMA calls a "compelling entry point." Higher growth and larger fiscal deficits imply higher real rates and larger term premia, pushing starting yields and embedded forward returns meaningfully higher. Context matters too. The LTCMA also raised our global equity forecast by 50bps to 7.5%, a constructive outlook in its own right. But the gap between equity and high-quality bond expected returns has narrowed sharply, and on a risk-adjusted basis the comparison now favours fixed income — sovereign bond Sharpe ratios have improved with higher starting yields and steeper curves, while equity Sharpe ratios are little changed. For investors used to thinking of bonds as a low-returning hedge, this is a regime change worth acting on. Starting yield has historically been one of the strongest predictors of forward bond returns. When yields have entered a period at today's levels, realised returns over the following several years have tended to cluster meaningfully higher than when starting yields were compressed — precisely the dynamic behind the LTCMA's two-decade-best forecasts. Past performance is never a guarantee, but the mechanics are simple. A higher coupon today compounds into a higher floor for total return tomorrow, and today's normalised real yields leave far less of that return dependent on price appreciation or duration risk. The hard work of waiting out the rate cycle has largely been done — the opportunity now is to earn the income. Fixed income continues to play a powerful role alongside equities. The LTCMA expects the correlation between global equities and U.S. aggregate bonds to be around 34% going forward, but it is explicit that "we still expect high-quality fixed income to have the lowest correlation to equities among liquid assets." Bonds remain a versatile tool: duration continues to be a strong hedge against demand-driven slowdowns, while inflation-linked and real assets can complement it when shocks come from the supply side. At the portfolio level, the math is compelling. The LTCMA's balanced global 60/40 stock-bond portfolio is projected to return 7.0%, up 60bp from last year's edition, with bonds contributing both income and ballast. This is a long-term, structural case for fixed income as a core allocation, not a tactical trade. Higher yields also make fixed income a more powerful planning tool — a meaningful, more predictable income stream can help investors fund specific long-term goals, such as retirement income, liability matching or legacy planning. Depending on their goals and preferences, investors can access this opportunity in many ways, from diversified bond funds and actively managed strategies to individual bond portfolios and ladders matched to future cash needs. Underpinning all of this is strong corporate fundamentals: issuers are often cash-rich and, per the LTCMA, "quite savvy in their debt management," supporting the case for high-quality credit. Economic nationalism is, per the LTCMA, "a modest growth risk but a greater risk to inflation." Elevated inflation volatility is expected to persist, particularly in higher-deficit nations such as the U.S., where continued deficits, debt brinkmanship and pressure on central bank independence could gradually weaken policy credibility and the "safe asset" premium. Supply chain, energy and security related themes are also current factors, which ideally calm. Credit markets are evolving too. Many governments face high debt, while corporations — often cash-rich and incentivized by shareholders to manage debt responsibly — now compare favourably on a relative risk basis. This quality theme has led the LTCMA to tighten its equilibrium credit spread assumptions, even as credit return projections generally keep pace with sovereign forecasts. On the upside, a genuine productivity renaissance driven by AI and a sustained investment super cycle could lift total factor productivity, limiting the rise in equilibrium real yields and supporting more stable, higher-quality returns across fixed income. Elevated yields, return forecasts at two-decade highs, lasting diversification benefits and strong corporate fundamentals add up to a compelling case. High-quality fixed income deserves a meaningful place in long-term, multi-asset, goals-based portfolios today. The opportunity is here, and investors can put it to work now, earning income levels not seen in a generation. Bond return forecasts are at two-decade highs, with structurally normalised real yields offering a compelling entry point. Investors can earn generation-high income levels now rather than waiting out further rate cycles. Key risks include economic nationalism and its pressure on inflation, persistent fiscal deficits weakening the "safe asset" premium and threats to central bank independence. Supply chain, energy and security-related themes are additional factors to monitor. The article doesn't address U.K. gilts specifically, but its broader thesis applies: higher starting sovereign yields globally translate into higher expected forward returns and a better income floor for long-term investors. While the article focuses on income rather than rate-cut scenarios, it notes duration remains a strong hedge against demand-driven slowdowns, implying price gains if rates fall amid weaker growth. High-quality fixed income is expected to retain the lowest correlation to equities among liquid assets, with a projected ~34% equity-bond correlation going forward. This supports bonds' role as ballast, helping the LTCMA's 60/40 portfolio forecast rise to 7.0%. Opportunities span U.S. Treasuries, investment grade and high-yield credit, and emerging market debt, each offering historically attractive yields and expected returns. The structural driver is normalised real yields and larger term premia from higher growth and fiscal deficits worldwide. title: J.P. Morgan Private Bank expanding in Dallas to tap alternative assets sector - TradingView
content: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, part of banking giant JPMorgan Chase JPM, is expanding its Fund Banking Group with a new hub in Dallas to serve the state's fast-growing private equity, venture capital, and hedge fund communities, the company said Wednesday. "Texas has become a genuine center of gravity for private equity, venture capital, and hedge funds," said Jeff Kaveney, head of Fund Banking at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. "The pace of growth for the region is remarkable, and this new Fund Banking hub responds directly to that momentum." JPMorgan Chase JPM has scaled the private bank platform quickly since it acquired First Republic Bank in 2023. The Private Bank has been serving the private and venture fund spaces and their CEO for 30 years, Kaveney added. The platform has roughly doubled in the past three years. The team now has 40 fund bankers with plans to expand by at least 20% in the next three years. First phase of industry-leading proof-of-concept demonstrates how signed mandates, verified identity, institutional controls and auditability can secure future agent-to-agent commerce. AI agents are moving from insight to action. Hyundai Card and Kinexys by J.P. Morgan, the firm’s industry-leading blockchain business unit of J.P. Morgan Payments, have collaborated to demonstrate that AI agents can safely participate in financial transactions when identity, delegated authority, controls, governance and auditability are directly embedded into institutional environments and payment flows. The future of commerce will increasingly involve AI agents acting on behalf of people, businesses and machines. A key question remains: can AI agents make a transaction safely, responsibly and with accountability? This phased proof-of-concept aims to establish the trust framework required for future agent-to-agent transactions as part of an agentic economy. Wee Kee Toh, Global Head of Kinexys Insights at Kinexys by J.P. Morgan, said, “Agentic commerce will not scale on autonomy alone. It will require trusted autonomy. Every autonomous action needs to be tied to a verified identity, a clear principal, a signed mandate and enforceable controls. This proof-of-concept shows how Kinexys can help provide the foundational trust, governance and execution framework that institutions need to explore AI agent transactions – whether that be one-to-one or one-to-many – in controlled environments. Starting with treasury, we see potential for this framework to support more complex agent-to-agent transaction models across connected commerce and machine-to-machine ecosystems.” Phase one focused on a treasury management use case in a test environment with no live value movement. Under a digitally signed AI agent mandate (“the mandate”), a Hyundai Card AI agent was tasked with autonomously managing Euro liquidity in Hyundai Card’s Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account in Frankfurt and requesting foreign exchange (FX) executions to maintain liquidity levels when required. The objective was to prove that AI agents can act on behalf of institutions under a signed, machine-readable mandate, while remaining subject to verified identity, delegated authority, institutional controls, human escalation and full auditability. In this use case – explored in further detail in this paper – Hyundai Card’s AI agent autonomously monitored the Blockchain Deposit Account balance, identified a Euro shortfall and determined that a Sterling Pound to Euro FX conversion was required to maintain the liquidity levels set out in the mandate. Hyundai Card’s AI agent then requested FX quotes and then engaged Kinexys for execution. Kinexys’ own AI agent then verified the identity and authority of the Hyundai Card AI agent and evaluated its request against the mandate and applicable controls. Based on this evaluation, the Kinexys AI agent could either auto-execute, escalate to a human for review, or deny the request. Following the evaluation, the Kinexys AI agent auto-executed the request and a simulated FX transaction was booked. Crucially, the complete reasoning and decision data was captured in an immutable audit trail, providing visibility into the end-to-end transaction flow. A Hyundai Card spokesperson said, “This proof-of-concept with Kinexys by J.P. Morgan is significant in that it validated a next-generation financial transaction model in which AI agents carry out corporate treasury management and foreign exchange transactions without direct human intervention. Building on our accumulated experience in payments in the mobility sector, we plan to expand our collaboration with Kinexys by J.P. Morgan into new areas such as payments in vehicles.” The proof-of-concept establishes key properties for the trust framework: Check out other recent news and insights on agentic commerce and agentic treasury: J.P. Morgan’s website and/or mobile terms, privacy and security policies don’t apply to the site or app you're about to visit. title: “Capital Has a Price Again,” Key Message from J.P. Morgan Private Bank for 2027 - Funds Society
content: Artificial intelligence, global fragmentation, and inflation are driving a historic repricing of capital, giving investors greater pricing power. This is the main conclusion of J.P. Morgan Private Bank’s 2027 global investment outlook report, “The Price of Progress.” “For much of the last cycle, investors could overlook the cost of capital. The next major phase of development demands paying closer attention to it. Today, technology companies, governments, and consumers compete for the same limited pool of capital, and it is investors who set its price. Every financing transaction must now clear a higher hurdle rate,” stated Grace Peters, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. For his part, Stephen Parker, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, added: “This pricing power puts investors in a position of strength, but it also makes capital allocation decisions carry greater consequences. Now that cash offers a real return, every investment must justify the capital allocated to it. The question is not simply where the opportunity lies, but where investors receive sufficient compensation for taking it on.” Regarding Europe, Oscar Carmona, Head of Investments at J.P. Morgan Private Bank in Spain, noted: “Europe has weathered rising energy costs and interest rates better than expected. We expect that resilience to hold in 2027. Inflation should moderate over time, but energy remains the decisive factor. If rising costs pass through to wages, food, and services, the downward path could be bumpy. We expect 2 additional rate hikes from the ECB, bringing the deposit facility rate (DFR) to 3% in early 2027, with limited room for much further tightening.” According to the firm, the “2027 Global Investment Outlook” report examines how investors must decide whom to lend to, which assets to invest in, and at what price, in an environment shaped by artificial intelligence, global fragmentation, and inflation. Throughout much of the post-financial crisis cycle, near-zero interest rates and quantitative easing policies kept financing costs low. However, this backdrop has changed. Inflation has remained above central bank targets throughout 2026, bond yields have reached multi-decade highs, and a global rate-hiking cycle has begun, with 17 of the 37 central banks we track currently oriented toward tightening monetary policy. Nevertheless, bond yields were already rising prior to monetary policy moves, underscoring the role investors now play in setting the price of capital. “Central banks will continue to play a pivotal role in 2027. How high rates go will matter, but policy rates do not tell the whole story. With investment-grade debt yields above 6% for the 1st time since the financial crisis, today’s starting point for high-credit-quality debt is more attractive than it has been in years, even if rates continue to rise,” Parker explained. He adds: “Higher yields reinforce the appeal of a traditional stock-and-bond portfolio, yet a balanced portfolio is only the starting point. Forward return outlooks for equities and fixed income are the most attractive in years, but uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence, inflation risk, and historically high equity market concentration justify going further. Real assets, hedge funds, and private markets have shifted from a complement to a necessity.” Security, resilience, and regional alignment are increasingly taking precedence over efficiency. Governments—many already carrying elevated debt levels and fiscal deficits—need capital to bolster security, build out artificial intelligence ecosystems, and secure energy supply. As these demands grow, investors must make increasingly consequential choices about where to provide capital and on what terms. In this context, Peters stated: “Resilience is an enduring investment theme, but it will not deliver uniform returns across all markets. Assessing countries’ defense and artificial intelligence capabilities, their exposure to supply chain bottlenecks, and their vulnerability to climate change can help identify where capital may be best positioned in this era of global fragmentation. Given that every bloc faces vulnerabilities, concentrating investments in just 1 is likely unwise.” She continues: “In the United States, fiscal capacity and natural resources continue to underpin confidence in U.S. Treasuries and the dollar, whereas stronger corporate earnings in Europe make equities more attractive than sovereign debt. In Asia, South Korea and Taiwan play an essential role in semiconductor manufacturing, while Latin America offers opportunities ranging from nearshoring in Mexico to commodity exposure in other countries across the region.” Artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion remains constrained by resource scarcity rather than excess capacity, yet the debate is shifting from infrastructure capacity toward monetization and political risks. By the early 2030s, the global fleet of data centers will need to generate approximately $3T annually in end-customer revenue to reach breakeven. That is an ambitious target, though we believe the AI ecosystem can achieve it. Meanwhile, AI-related debt issuance is expected to exceed $300B this year. While it remains predominantly investment-grade debt, the emergence of newer, less transparent structures is driving up the cost of AI financing. “The boom can only continue if investors bridge the gap between infrastructure spending and sustainable revenue generation. Not every segment of the AI technology stack carries the same level of risk or warrants the same capital allocation. This requires making deliberate choices about where to invest within the AI ecosystem, rather than simply whether to participate in it,” Parker clarified. We believe hyperscalers offer the best exposure within public equities due to their ability to benefit from both compute scarcity and abundance scenarios. Conversely, the infrastructure and semiconductor segments warrant greater caution, particularly given growing political hurdles to data center construction. Regarding investment-grade AI-related debt, it provides the best risk-managed entry point, while the application layer, frontier AI labs, and AI-native software offer the most compelling long-term growth potential, best accessed selectively through private markets.
